## import Data

```{r}
# read the csv file (keep it in the same folder as this Rmd file)
students <- read.csv("C:\\Users\\HP\\Desktop\\Study\\Hw\\StudentsPerformance.csv")

# see the first 6 rows
head(students)

# how many rows and columns
dim(students)

# summary of the three scores I will use
summary(students[, c("math.score", "reading.score", "writing.score")])

# check if there are missing values (0 means none)
sum(is.na(students))
```


```{r}
# writing score vs math score
plot(students$math.score, students$writing.score,
     xlab = "Math score", ylab = "Writing score",
     main = "Writing vs Math")

# writing score vs reading score
plot(students$reading.score, students$writing.score,
     xlab = "Reading score", ylab = "Writing score",
     main = "Writing vs Reading")

# correlation between the three scores
cor(students[, c("math.score", "reading.score", "writing.score")])
```

Both plots go upwards, so students who score high in math or reading also tend
to score high in writing. The correlation between reading and writing is very
strong (about 0.95) and math and writing is also strong (about 0.80).

```{r}
# lm() fits the multiple linear regression
model <- lm(writing.score ~ math.score + reading.score, data = students)

# show the results
summary(model)
```
## Interpretation

The fitted model is:

writing score = -1.16 + 0.067 x math score + 0.937 x reading score

- **math.score (0.067):** If reading score stays the same, one extra point in math adds about 0.07 points to the writing score. It is significant (p < 0.001), but the effect is small.
- **reading.score (0.937):** If math score stays the same, one extra point in reading adds about 0.94 points to the writing score. It is significant (p < 0.001) and it is the main predictor.
- **Intercept (-1.16):** This is the predicted writing score when math and reading are both 0. It is not significant (p > 0.05) and has no real meaning here.
- **R-squared (0.913):** Math and reading together explain about 91% of the differences in writing scores, so the model fits very well.
- **F-test:** The p-value is less than 0.001, so the model is significant overall.
- **Residual standard error (4.49):** Predictions are off by about 4.5 points on average.

**Conclusion:** Reading score is the strongest predictor of writing score. Math score also helps but adds very little.


## Check the assumptions

```{r}
# 4 diagnostic plots in one picture
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

From the plots, the residuals are mostly close to the line in the Q-Q plot and
the points in the residuals vs fitted plot are spread around zero without a
strong pattern, so the model is acceptable. A few students with very low scores
show up as outliers.


```{r predict}
# predict the writing score of a student with math = 70 and reading = 75
new_student <- data.frame(math.score = 70, reading.score = 75)
predict(model, newdata = new_student)
```

The predicted writing score is about 74.
